title: Assessment method: turn a feature into a test
model: Start with a business rule rather than a vulnerability name. Identify actor, asset, entry point, trust boundary and consequence. For an invoice feature, the rule is that each user can read only invoices belonging to the permitted tenant and owner.
setup: Create an endpoint inventory with method, inputs, authentication state, role, object ownership and state-changing effects. Prioritize sensitive workflows such as account recovery and payments. Agree scope, request limits and a stop condition before connecting tools.
workflow: Choose one known-good request and one changed condition. Keep other variables constant. Use a synthetic record and a second account; preserve a legitimate operation as a control. Repeat after resetting relevant state.
evidence: An unexpected status alone is weak evidence. Confirm response content, identity and resulting server state. Record untested branches instead of marking the entire feature secure.
tools: Burp HTTP history, browser Network panel and a request matrix support inventory; a scanner cannot infer every business rule.
repair: Repair the violated invariant at the server boundary. Retest the original case plus an allowed case and any equivalent endpoint.
practice: Use the casebook invoice matrix: Alice-own, Alice-other, Bob-own and anonymous. Explain the result of each before running automation.

title: Burp workflow: controlled comparisons
model: A proxy records traffic; Repeater lets you isolate and replay a particular exchange. Authentication state and workflow context determine whether two requests are comparable.
setup: Scope only the configured lab origin. Browse a known feature, send its request to Repeater and keep a baseline tab. Label tabs by actor and object, not token values. Disable unnecessary automatic behavior that hides redirects or state transitions.
workflow: Change one identifier or writable field. Inspect request headers, body type, response identity and side effects. Renew expired fixture tokens before attributing a difference to a vulnerability. Compare raw content when visual rendering hides fields.
evidence: A response-size difference may reflect a timestamp, CSRF nonce or language setting. A redirect may lead to login. Evidence must isolate the security-relevant difference.
tools: Proxy/history provides context; Repeater handles manual tests; Comparer highlights differences. Intruder is for a small reviewed input set with explicit limits, not a substitute for a hypothesis.
repair: Keep a redacted baseline and changed request. After a fix, verify both unauthorized denial and the baseline operation.
practice: Use the Chapter 38 fixture to change invoice 1 to 2 under the same Alice token; then test invoice 2 under Bob separately.

title: Discovery: paths, parameters and false positives
model: Discovery maps potential inputs. A found route is not automatically a vulnerability, and a guessed path can trigger an action on poorly designed services.
setup: Begin with browser-observed routes, API contracts and supplied source. For bounded lab enumeration, establish an unknown-path baseline first and use a tiny reviewed wordlist. Record redirects without silently following them across scope.
workflow: Compare status, length, content type and stable body markers. If every path returns the same login page, report that behavior rather than hundreds of discovered endpoints. Separate anonymous and authenticated observations.
evidence: Filtering all responses of one length can hide real content. A 403 can establish a denied route, but does not prove bypass or sensitive exposure. Version fingerprints need confirmation.
tools: ffuf or Gobuster can send the small input set; curl verifies individual candidates. Wappalyzer hints at technology but does not prove patch status.
repair: Remove unused exposed routes where appropriate; enforce authorization on required routes. Repeat discovery and manual access tests after remediation.
practice: The tool workbook uses only strong, weak, redirect and missing against the supplied loopback fixture. Expected statuses are 200, 200, 302 and 404.

title: Authentication, recovery and session state
model: Model login, MFA, recovery and session renewal as explicit states. Possession of a pending token must not imply completion of MFA. Recovery is an authentication path, not merely an email feature.
setup: List the permissions granted in each state and the invalidation events. Test synthetic accounts for pending-session access, token rotation, old-token reuse, logout and expiry. Keep recovery delivery inside a controlled fixture.
workflow: Compare protected reads before and after each transition. Inspect the server identity and token validity rather than relying on a changed cookie. For password reset, separately review expiry, one-time use and binding to the intended account.
evidence: Different error messages are observations; demonstrate whether they reveal useful account information in context. A generic message alone does not establish timing equivalence or a secure recovery flow.
tools: Burp Repeater and the existing auth exercise cover state transitions. The toy MFA code is public and does not model a real second factor or identity provider.
repair: Enforce complete authentication centrally; rotate and invalidate session credentials at appropriate transitions. Revoke recovery artifacts atomically after use.
practice: Run exercise.py --expect fixed --case auth in the casebook, then read test_wrong_mfa_code and test_expired_session to identify what remains untested.

title: Authorization across objects, tenants and functions
model: Authentication answers who is calling. Authorization asks whether that actor may perform this operation on this object in its current state.
setup: Create a matrix covering anonymous, owner, other owner, another tenant and administrator where supported. Include read, update, delete, export and list paths. Do not invent supported roles when the fixture has none.
workflow: Start with two known synthetic objects and two identities. Change only the object while holding the actor fixed, then restore the object and change the actor. Verify server state for write operations.
evidence: Random identifiers make guessing harder but do not prove authorization. A 404 can intentionally conceal forbidden resources; verify that protected data and effects are absent.
tools: Burp tabs or the supplied Postman collection organize the matrix. Python tests preserve it as a regression suite.
repair: Use a centralized policy and scoped data queries; avoid accepting owner or tenant authority directly from request fields. Retest all equivalent access paths.
practice: Contrast the vulnerable and fixed invoice fixture. A denied item endpoint does not by itself prove the collection or retired version is protected.

title: SQL injection: data crossing into query syntax
model: SQL injection occurs when untrusted input changes the structure of a database statement. The key distinction is query structure versus bound data, not whether the input contains unusual characters.
setup: Trace an input from HTTP parsing through validation to the database API. Identify concatenated SQL, dynamic identifiers and privilege of the database connection. Establish a valid input and an absent-result control.
workflow: Use the supplied in-memory SQLite demonstration to compare a normal owner lookup with a teaching input that changes a concatenated predicate. Run the same inputs through the parameterized implementation and compare returned rows.
evidence: A database error or scanner label alone does not establish data exposure. Differences may come from validation or caching. Parameter placeholders typically bind values, not arbitrary table names or sort expressions.
tools: Python sqlite3 and source review show the root cause directly. sqlmap is an optional SQLi assessment tool for a separately authorized, resettable database lab; no extraction or destructive workflow is needed here.
repair: Bind values, allowlist any required dynamic identifiers and minimize database privileges. Retest ordinary names containing apostrophes as well as the original teaching input.
practice: Run boundary_lab.py and its tests from examples/web-deep-dive. The database contains only synthetic invoice rows and exists in memory.

title: XSS: source, sink and output context
model: Untrusted text becomes dangerous when interpreted as executable browser content. Reflected, stored and DOM-based describe different delivery paths; the actual sink and context determine the repair.
setup: Use a harmless unique text marker to trace where input appears. Inspect raw responses, the live DOM and the JavaScript code assigning the value. Identify HTML text, attributes, URLs, JavaScript or CSS contexts separately.
workflow: Compare a text node assignment with an HTML-parsing assignment in code. For stored input, trace the later viewer and rendering path, not only the submission response. Keep any browser proof confined to a lab without external callbacks.
evidence: Reflection alone is not XSS. HTML encoding suitable for a text node is not a general JavaScript, URL or CSS defense. CSP can reduce impact but does not repair an unsafe sink.
tools: Browser developer tools identify DOM transformations; Burp compares responses; source analysis traces data to innerHTML or equivalent framework escape hatches.
repair: Prefer safe text APIs and framework escaping; use a suitable maintained sanitizer only when rich HTML is required. Retest rendering and legitimate content.
practice: The offline exercise demonstrates HTML text escaping with a markup-looking string. It does not run JavaScript and cannot certify a browser page free of XSS.

title: CSRF: request authority and browser behavior
model: CSRF exploits a browser automatically sending credentials with an unwanted state-changing request. Reading the response is not necessary for an unwanted action.
setup: Inventory which operations mutate state, which credentials are automatic, and whether anti-CSRF tokens are tied to the session. Check origin validation and SameSite behavior against actual application flows.
workflow: In an isolated browser lab, compare a legitimate change with missing, invalid and other-session tokens. Inspect both network results and the changed server state. Consider allowed methods and content types.
evidence: A request rejected by CORS may still have reached the server. Conversely, a manually replayed request outside a browser does not prove a cross-site browser attack is possible.
tools: Browser Network panel establishes browser sending behavior; Repeater checks server token validation. Keep these two kinds of evidence separate.
repair: Use framework CSRF protections for cookie-authenticated state changes, validate request origins where appropriate and avoid state changes through safe-method endpoints.
practice: Create a worksheet for a profile change: valid token, missing token and other-session token. The existing casebook uses explicit bearer headers and is not a cookie-CSRF lab.

title: CORS: readable responses versus server access
model: CORS is a browser response-sharing policy. It is not API authentication and does not stop ordinary non-browser clients from sending HTTP requests.
setup: Record allowed origins, credential behavior, preflight decisions and the sensitivity of the actual response. Distinguish an exact approved origin from unconstrained reflection.
workflow: Send a single harmless Origin header to the local /cors fixture. Inspect Access-Control-Allow-Origin and Access-Control-Allow-Credentials. A full impact proof would additionally require a browser, usable credentials and sensitive content.
evidence: Reflected Origin headers alone do not establish private data theft. The supplied response is fictional public HTML and has no real authenticated user data.
tools: curl shows headers; browser developer tools show enforcement. ZAP passive alerts are observations to validate, not proof of authorization failure.
repair: Allow only required origins, separate public responses from credentialed ones and verify cache variation where responses differ by Origin.
practice: Compare /cors and /strong using the workbook commands. Report the fixture as a permissive policy demonstration, not a confirmed account compromise.

title: SSRF: server-side fetch trust boundaries
model: SSRF occurs when untrusted input directs server-side requests beyond intended destinations or behavior. The server network identity may reach resources a browser cannot.
setup: Identify URL importers, image fetchers, webhook validators and document converters. Map parsing, resolution, connection and redirect handling. Define permitted schemes, hosts and destinations.
workflow: Use an owned local receiver returning a benign marker to establish whether a fetch happens. Record the source context and whether the response is returned. A redirect test requires reviewing the new destination as well.
evidence: A URL-looking parameter is not proof of a fetch. DNS resolution alone does not prove an HTTP request or access to sensitive data. Do not probe metadata endpoints to demonstrate a generic concept.
tools: A local HTTP receiver, application logs and source review are sufficient for controlled evidence. The handbook REST fixture has no URL-fetch feature.
repair: Constrain fetch destinations, enforce egress policy, validate every redirect and address resolution, and avoid passing ambient credentials to fetched destinations.
practice: Draw parse -> resolve -> policy -> connect -> redirect for a fictional importer. Mark where DNS rebinding and redirect changes require implementation-specific protection.

title: File upload and path traversal
model: Upload handling combines file naming, content parsing, storage, retrieval and permissions. Traversal occurs when an input path escapes an intended storage boundary.
setup: Map the complete lifecycle: size limits, content checks, server-generated identifiers, storage location, parser behavior, download authorization and response headers. A filename extension is only a hint.
workflow: Use a tiny inert text file with a unique marker. Test allowed retrieval and another account denial. In code review, check canonical path handling and symlink behavior rather than searching only for the literal ../ sequence.
evidence: Accepting a file with a surprising extension is not necessarily execution. A path error does not establish an outside-root read. Never use a real sensitive file as proof when a synthetic sentinel suffices.
tools: Burp inspects multipart requests; file and hashes identify lab artifacts; source review verifies storage and retrieval boundaries.
repair: Use opaque file identifiers, storage outside executable web paths, appropriate content processing and authorization on every retrieval. Address race conditions between checking and opening files.
practice: Write tests for a permitted synthetic upload, oversized input, malformed content and cross-user retrieval. This topic needs a separate upload fixture; the supplied server has no upload endpoint.

title: Business logic and state machines
model: A business flaw violates an invariant such as paid orders alone may be fulfilled or a coupon may be redeemed once. Valid HTTP and valid JSON can still violate the rule.
setup: Draw states and permitted transitions, including cancellation, retry and recovery. Identify which actor may trigger each transition and which values must come from server records.
workflow: Attempt one out-of-order transition in an in-memory model, then a valid sequence. Check durable effects and whether retries duplicate work. Do not confuse client-visible state with authoritative stored state.
evidence: A hidden button is not a state guard. A rejected request is not enough if part of its effect occurred first. Confirm the final order or balance state.
tools: Python unit tests are well suited to transition matrices. Burp observes the corresponding API workflow when a resettable HTTP lab exists.
repair: Enforce transition preconditions and atomic state changes at the authoritative service; recompute sensitive totals from trusted data.
practice: The new offline lab contrasts a fulfillment function that ignores payment with a guarded transition. The example has no payment gateway and no concurrency guarantees.

title: Race conditions, idempotency and atomicity
model: A race arises when overlapping operations violate a shared invariant. Idempotency and atomicity are related but distinct: retrying one logical operation should not duplicate its effect, and competing operations must not both consume the same resource.
setup: Identify read-check-write sequences, transaction boundaries and idempotency-key scope. Define what should happen when the same request or two distinct requests arrive together.
workflow: Use the existing deterministic race demonstration and fixture redemption test. Compare final counts and server state rather than inferring a race from request timing alone.
evidence: Sending two requests does not prove they overlapped at the vulnerable section. Network scheduling can hide or invent apparent differences; deterministic barriers make local model tests more useful.
tools: Python controlled concurrency tests establish the local invariant. Manual proxy tools help inspect the HTTP contract, but test a bounded number of requests.
repair: Use suitable database constraints, transactions or atomic primitives. Scope idempotency records to actor and operation, bind them to relevant inputs and define their lifetime.
practice: Run race_demo.py and test_atomic_http_redemption in the existing casebook. Its in-memory lock is a teaching mechanism, not a multi-process database design.

title: Caches, personalization and response confusion
model: A cache reuses a stored response using a cache key. A vulnerability can arise when response-affecting inputs or user identity are absent from that key or private content is stored incorrectly.
setup: Identify browser, CDN, reverse proxy and application caches separately. Record cache controls, variation, authentication state and whether the response is personalized.
workflow: In a dedicated local cache lab, use a unique harmless marker and two synthetic users. Observe repeat requests and response identity; reset the cache between cases to isolate key behavior.
evidence: Age, timing or a cache header alone does not prove poisoning or leakage. The fixture here has no shared proxy cache, so its headers cannot reproduce a cache-key vulnerability.
tools: curl preserves headers and redirects; Repeater supports paired requests. Application or proxy logs establish whether a response came from cache.
repair: Separate public and private responses, define correct key variation and avoid caching sensitive authenticated output when inappropriate. Retest across users and key variants.
practice: Write a cache test matrix: anonymous, Alice, Bob, path, query and Origin. State which dimensions should affect the response and which should affect its cache key.

title: HTTP parser boundaries and request smuggling
model: Request smuggling involves disagreement about message boundaries between components such as a frontend proxy and backend server. Testing can affect other requests sharing a connection.
setup: Map every HTTP hop, protocol translation and connection reuse policy. Review component documentation and patch status. Treat a single-server parser test as limited evidence.
workflow: Use only a dedicated isolated proxy/backend lab for active experiments. First establish ordinary connection behavior and collect logs from both sides. This book provides architecture reasoning, not ambiguous framing payloads against shared services.
evidence: A timeout or 400 is not proof of desynchronization. A valid conclusion needs correlated evidence that components interpreted boundaries differently. The Python fixture is not a smuggling lab.
tools: Proxy/server logs and controlled packet captures help compare interpretations. Specialized extensions require understanding their request generation and impact before use.
repair: Keep components updated and configure consistent message parsing and protocol handling; verify rejection behavior across the whole chain.
practice: Draw client -> proxy -> backend, annotate where lengths and framing are interpreted, then list what evidence would distinguish a parser error from cross-request confusion.

title: Code review: connect an input to a dangerous operation
model: A source pattern becomes a vulnerability only when relevant untrusted input can reach a sensitive operation without an effective control. Reachability and execution context matter.
setup: Map route to parser, validator, policy decision, database or rendering sink, and response. Inspect alternate branches and helper functions rather than a single suspicious line.
workflow: Run the supplied Semgrep rule on the supplied teaching source without executing it. Trace the reported eval input manually and propose a constrained parser or explicit operation dispatch.
evidence: Pattern matching can miss aliases and wrappers or flag trusted input. A clean scan is not proof of safe authorization, business logic or every data flow.
tools: Semgrep provides candidate locations; an editor and unit tests confirm behavior. Dependency and secret scanners answer different questions and need separate evidence.
repair: Repair the data flow or remove the dangerous primitive, then add a regression for the original path and valid input. Do not merely suppress the warning.
practice: Use review-eval.yaml and sample_review.py from examples/advanced-web. Compare the flagged teaching source with a copy that uses an appropriate safe parser.

title: Automation: tests, templates and negative controls
model: Automation repeats explicit assumptions. A template match establishes its matcher condition; a security conclusion also needs affected context and impact.
setup: Read the request, redirects, matchers and any external interactions before executing a template. Use one local target and a reviewed local template; bound concurrency and rate.
workflow: Run the supplied informational header template against the fixture. Copy it and change the path from /strong to /weak: the specific nosniff observation should no longer match.
evidence: No match can mean an expired session, wrong path, unavailable service or filter mismatch. A positive header match is not an exploitable vulnerability.
tools: Nuclei supports reviewed HTTP templates; Python handles semantic regression assertions; Postman preserves an explicit API request sequence.
repair: Keep test expectations tied to the policy, fail clearly on setup errors and record tool versions. Verify a negative control before relying on a new check.
practice: The workbook gives the local Nuclei and Semgrep commands. These optional tools are not installed or executed by the website.

title: Reporting: make evidence support a repair
model: A useful finding explains a violated rule, prerequisites, minimal reproduction, observed effect and why that effect matters to this application.
setup: Distinguish confirmed behavior, likely consequence and untested inference. Use synthetic records and redact credentials. Record role, version, endpoint, time and state needed to reproduce the result.
workflow: Write a baseline/changed/retest table. Include one allowed action after the fix so reviewers can see the repair did not disable the feature. Record partial fixes and untested equivalent paths.
evidence: Scanner severity is not automatically business severity. A missing header and cross-tenant data access require different evidence and impact assessment. Avoid claiming complete coverage from a small suite.
tools: Use the downloadable assessment worksheet and existing report template. Request IDs and normalized response differences are more helpful than screenshots full of tokens.
repair: Assign a root-cause repair, confirm the exact changed behavior and identify remaining risk. Preserve evidence securely according to the engagement rules.
practice: Finish by producing one BOLA finding from vulnerable mode and its fixed-mode retest, with Alice-own and Bob-own requests still succeeding.
